Adult individuals of the Striped venus clam Chamelea gallina typically attain a maximum shell length of 4.4 centimeters [Li = 4.4 centimeters], a size that defines the upper boundary of somatic growth for this commercially important bivalve. Field surveys within the Adriatic Sea consistently indicate that the onset of reproductive capability is marked by the attainment of a total length at puberty of 1.03 centimeters [Lp = 1.03 centimeters]. Growth trajectory analyses demonstrate that individuals reach this critical developmental threshold during their first year of life, after which energetic resources are progressively diverted toward gametogenesis rather than exclusively toward shell accretion. The ability to achieve such a modest pubertal size within a relatively brief post-settlement period is characteristic of many infaunal bivalves inhabiting highly productive coastal environments, where early reproduction can enhance lifetime fitness despite the associated trade-offs with continued somatic expansion.

Long-term laboratory rearing experiments conducted at a stable ambient temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] have provided robust empirical estimates for several fundamental life-history parameters in Chamelea gallina. Under these controlled thermal conditions, the age at birth, defined as the interval from egg fertilisation through embryonated egg development to the eclosion of the first free-swimming veliger larva, was recorded at approximately 2.17 days [ab = approximately 2.17 days] at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This relatively abbreviated embryonic phase is consistent with the rapid developmental rates observed in many warm-temperate bivalves with planktotrophic larval strategies. Furthermore, the same thermal regime supports an extended maximum recorded lifespan, with the oldest documented individuals reaching approximately 16425 days [am = approximately 16425 days] before succumbing to natural senescence at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Such longevity is notable among members of the Veneridae, reflecting a slow-paced adult somatic maintenance regime and a reproductive strategy that distributes spawning effort across numerous consecutive seasons.

The wet weight at birth for Chamelea gallina, corresponding to the mass of the newly hatched veliger larva immediately following hatching, is an exceedingly low 0.14 micrograms [Wwb = 0.14 micrograms]. This minuscule initial mass is computed from the approximate diameter of the yolk-laden egg, which measures roughly 65 micrometers, and highlights the extreme planktotrophic dependence of the early larval stages. In stark contrast, the ultimate wet weight that a fully grown adult can achieve under favorable environmental conditions is 19.9 grams [Wwi = 19.9 grams]. This represents a mass increase exceeding eight orders of magnitude from the larval stage to the reproductively active adult, a trajectory that underscores the prodigious filtering capacity and assimilation efficiency of this species. The vast disparity between neonatal and asymptotic body mass is a common feature among marine bivalves that exhibit planktotrophic development and filter-feeding throughout their benthic juvenile and adult phases.

Reproductive output in Chamelea gallina has been quantified through detailed histological and volumetric analyses of gonadal tissue in specimens collected from natural populations. Field data indicate that a female at a standard shell length of 3 centimeters achieves a maximum daily reproductive rate of approximately 2,184 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 2,184 eggs per day] when the water temperature is 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This high fecundity reflects a strategy of producing numerous small, yolk-deficient oocytes that are fertilised externally during broadcast spawning events. Such elevated partial fecundity, coupled with the extended adult lifespan, yields a substantial lifetime reproductive output that contributes to the species' ecological success and commercial abundance in sandy sublittoral habitats of the Mediterranean and adjacent Atlantic coasts.

Comparisons across congeneric species within the Veneridae reveal that the life-history traits of Chamelea gallina are well-adapted to the stochastic recruitment environment characteristic of temperate coastal zones. The relatively rapid developmental rate observed at 20 °C [T = 20 °C] ensures that the age at birth remains brief, minimizing the pelagic larval duration and thereby reducing the risk of advective losses from suitable settlement habitats. Meanwhile, the maximum recorded longevity of approximately 16425 days [am = approximately 16425 days] provides multiple opportunities for reproductive contribution across several spawning seasons, buffering against years of poor recruitment due to unfavorable hydrographic conditions or food limitation at a temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. The ultimate shell length of 4.4 centimeters [Li = 4.4 centimeters] positions this species as a medium-sized venerid, a size that balances the energetic demands of somatic tissue production with the allocation of resources necessary to sustain the observed high fecundity rates, ultimately shaping its population dynamics and resilience to fishing pressure.
